data.title: China's AI Migration
data.description:
Text｜Sleepy

There is a pattern in industrial history: the closer we get to a new generation, the clearer it becomes where a technology truly originated.

In England during the 1760s and 1770s, water-powered spinning machines had just been invented. Factory owners headed north to find valleys in Derbyshire and Lancashire on either side of the Pennine Mountains. At that time, Watt's steam engine had not yet entered textile factories; water turbines were still used to power the spindles. A few decades later, steam engines became widespread, and factories gradually moved from valleys to coalfields and the outskirts of cities.

Every technological advancement begins with the invention of an algorithm, a blueprint, or a machine, followed by a massive geographical relocation involving the search for electricity, water, and land. When times are calm, the global supply chain resembles a smooth net, and computing power can be mobilized even across the Pacific Ocean. This easily creates the illusion that software and intelligence are weightless and undemanding. However, once blockades and restrictions are encountered, the cloud returns to the ground, revealing its true nature as heavy industry: it requires electricity, is sensitive to heat, is particular about power lines, and, most importantly, depends on the manufacturer of the chips housed in those rows of server racks. On October 16, 1964, at Lop Nur, China successfully detonated its first atomic bomb, codenamed "596". Five years earlier, on June 20, 1959, the Central Committee of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union sent a letter to the Central Committee of the Communist Party of China, deciding to temporarily suspend the provision of the atomic bomb teaching models and blueprints agreed upon in the agreement.

Mushroom cloud from the explosion of China's first atomic bomb in Lop Nur in 1964 | Image source: People's Pictorial

Almost in the same autumn, the site selection policy for the Third Front construction was set: near mountains, dispersed, and concealed. In practice, two more words were added: underground. Over the next decade, millions of workers, cadres, intellectuals, and PLA soldiers left the cities of the east and northeast, moving machine tools, blast furnaces, and laboratories into the mountains of the southwest and northwest. At its peak, more than 4 million people were involved. More than half a century has passed, and the world's most cutting-edge industries have been replaced by large-scale models. Those training these large models have a daily routine: saving checkpoints. Thousands or even tens of thousands of accelerator cards run continuously for months; if even one card disconnects, training is interrupted. Every so often, all the model's weights, optimizer states, and random number seeds are saved so that if a problem occurs, training can resume from the most recent node. This word also has a literal meaning in English: border checkpoint. In November 2026, after a long search across the equator, China's large model industry finally reached its checkpoint. The story begins with four suitcases bound for Kuala Lumpur. In early March 2025, four Chinese engineers flew from Beijing to Malaysia. Each of them carried a suitcase containing 15 hard drives, totaling 80TB of data. Their destination was a data center in Malaysia, where their employer had rented approximately 300 servers equipped with advanced NVIDIA chips. For this flight, their colleagues back home began refining the dataset and repeatedly debugging the training program more than eight weeks in advance. Once the data is packed into boxes and leaves the country, it's difficult to start over as easily as it would be back home in a foreign server room. The reason for not transferring it over the network was that network transmission "might take several months," making physical transfer faster. According to the plan, what they ultimately wanted to bring back was much smaller, only a few hundred gigabytes—the trained model parameters. This is the most basic aspect of the first large-scale computing power migration in China; if the data can't get in, it has to be shipped out. What forced the engineers to take to the airport was the increasingly stringent chip ban over the past few years. On October 7, 2022, the US banned the sale of Nvidia A100 and H100 chips to China for the first time; Nvidia quickly modified the A800 and H800 specifically for the Chinese market, reducing interconnect bandwidth. Just one year later, on October 17, 2023, even the slower versions were shut out.

2022 and 2023 US Advanced Computing Chip Export Control Rules | Image Source: Government Website

That year, domestic market demand for advanced computing chips was extremely high. The price of the A100 jumped from around 40,000 yuan at the beginning of the year to nearly 250,000 yuan; in the week after the new regulations were implemented in October, the price of the H800 almost doubled, with a complete 8-card system being quoted as 2.45 million yuan by distributors.

At the same time, domestic computing infrastructure experienced a premature development. Between 2023 and 2024, more than 500 intelligent computing center projects were announced across various regions, with at least 150 already operational by the end of 2024. On one hand, labs were struggling to purchase GPUs despite having cash, while on the other hand, server rooms across the country were vacant. This was due to the physical barriers to training large-scale models. Cutting-edge models require tens of thousands of high-end GPUs of the same generation connected to a large cluster via a high-speed network. However, the server rooms scattered across the country mostly contained fragmented, outdated, and poorly connected inference cards or older-generation graphics cards. Fortunately, at the time, US export controls had a loophole, allowing only buying and selling, not leasing. Companies headquartered in China couldn't import chips into the country, but they could rent data centers from overseas cloud providers and non-Chinese owners. The industry quickly devised a division of labor: pre-training, which demands the most computing power and requires the highest cluster communication bandwidth, was done in overseas data centers; once the model was trained, the weights were brought back to China, where domestic computing power pools handled daily user inference. Once this approach worked, the rudimentary method of carrying suitcases was quickly replaced by modern cloud infrastructure. Later, engineers no longer needed to travel abroad. The training cluster remains in data centers in Southeast Asia or Northern Europe, while the algorithm team remotely logs in from their workstations in Beijing's Haidian District, Hangzhou's Yuhang District, or Shanghai's Xuhui District, typing out start-up commands in their terminals. There is an invisible aerial corridor on Earth called the "East Asia-Australasian Flyway." It originates in the Russian Far East and Alaska, traverses East and Southeast Asia, and extends to Australia and New Zealand, passing through 22 countries. More than 50 million waterbirds migrate along it every year. The mangrove wetlands on the southwest coast of Johor, Malaysia, are one of the rest stops along this route, with Tanjung Piai being the southernmost point of the Asian continent. Over the past five years, a new species of silicon-based migratory bird has appeared on this flyway. Johor is separated from Singapore only by the narrow Johor Strait. The red soil here has been transformed with several crops. In the 1940s, Chinese families arriving from Singapore cleared the tropical rainforest to plant pepper and gambier; British colonists arrived and changed the crops to rubber; by the second half of the 20th century, the hillsides were covered with oil palm trees. Today, bulldozers have cleared vast tracts of oil palm forests and planted Johor's fourth-generation cash crop: data centers. [Image source: D.W. Fisher-Freberg] In 2021, the entire state of Johor had only 10MW of online IT load. By the end of 2025, this number will exceed 900MW. What attracts people is the stark difference in factor prices between the two sides of the Taiwan Strait. Singapore, with its limited land and expensive electricity, suspended approvals for new data centers between 2019 and 2022. In contrast, in Johor's Seniana Technology Park across the Strait, land costs only S$5.12 per square foot, while in Singapore's Taichung area it's around S$6,000; Johor's electricity prices are also only about half of Singapore's. What surprises overseas counterparts even more is the delivery speed of Chinese infrastructure teams. Chinese-funded operators can acquire land, level it, connect electricity, install cooling systems, and turn on the lights to hand over the data center in nine to twelve months. DayOne and Bridge Data Centres, which merged with Chindata and is now owned by US capital, together hold at least 58% of Johor's online IT capacity. Among the Chinese operators in Johor, ByteDance is the largest customer. The causeway connecting Johor Bahru and Woodlands, Singapore, sees hundreds of thousands of people checking documents daily, making it one of the world's busiest land border crossings and the most famous physical checkpoint in the area. Meanwhile, in data centers on both sides of the strait, another type of checkpoint is being stored on hard drives. In November 2025, the Financial Times reported that both Alibaba and ByteDance were training their latest models in data centers in Southeast Asia, under leases with non-Chinese owners. A Singaporean data center operator explained to the media at the time, "Training cutting-edge models requires the best chips, and everything is legal and compliant." The US think tank IFP estimated that by the end of 2026, Chinese companies could mobilize computing power equivalent to approximately 1 million H100 servers through overseas remote access, with about 75% of that distributed in Southeast Asia. Since 2021, Malaysia has approved a cumulative total of US$95 billion in data center investments. The farthest-flying team reached the edge of the Arctic Circle. Starting in May 2025, an overseas subsidiary of ByteDance rented 2,304 Nvidia B200 chips in Gromfjør, a fjord town in northern Norway. The town relies on hydroelectric power and experiences consistently low temperatures. This single order from ByteDance accounted for approximately three-quarters of the European company Neocloud's revenue that year. But everyone knows that a borrowed roof cannot shelter you from prolonged rain. Migratory birds fly south, never intending to settle in the south. Both companies faced a similar challenge of being surrounded by computing power. Between 2025 and 2026, Kimi and DeepSeek, two of China's most representative large-scale model companies, took two different paths. On the path of searching for computing power in the south, Dark Side of the Moon was the most aggressive. In the words of an insider, their global search for computing power was "very aggressive." In July 2025, Dark Side of the Moon released K2 with 1 trillion parameters, completing pre-training on 15.5 trillion tokens using its self-developed MuonClip optimizer. A year later, on July 16, 2026, K3 was officially released, pushing the total number of parameters to 2.8 trillion, making it the world's first 3T-level model with open weights. American AI scholar Nathan Lambert specifically mentioned in his evaluation of K3 that this model was created "in a GPU-constrained environment." He jokingly mentioned to researchers at Kimi that at OpenAI, an average researcher might have "several thousand H100 equivalent machines," which "shocked" them. With far fewer cards than their Silicon Valley counterparts, the Chinese team delivered a result that cannot be ignored across the ocean. A November 2026 enterprise-level report released by Silicon Valley venture capital firm Menlo Ventures showed that 89% of the money spent by US companies on open-source big models flowed to Chinese models, with Kimi alone taking 61% of that share. Menlo Ventures 2026 Enterprise AI Report | Image Source: Menlo Ventures

Menlo Ventures 2026 Enterprise AI Report｜Image Source: Menlo Ventures

The most direct problem with powerful models is that there aren't enough memory cards.

Just three days after the K3 release, on July 19th, Kimi officially posted a "Statement Regarding the Shortage of Computing Power and the Suspension of Membership," stating that in the past 48 hours, user requests had far exceeded expectations, approaching the capacity limit of the existing cluster.

The new membership channel had to be temporarily closed, with new memberships to be released in batches once a new batch of computing power arrived. To alleviate the pressure on the inference cluster, Dark Side of the Moon used every conceivable method. They partnered with several US cloud providers to host K3 revenue sharing, leveraging their open-source influence to have overseas cloud providers use their own GPUs to handle overseas enterprise clients for Kimi. However, pre-training the next-generation flagship model cannot be solved by offloading resources. According to a report by The Information in late July, the planned K4 will be much larger than K3. Dark Side of the Moon turned its attention to Indonesia, signing a lease worth approximately $150 million for an NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra B300 cluster in an Indonesian data center, planned to be operational as early as 2027. Reportedly, these cards are specifically intended for K4. While the dark side of the moon was scrambling to find credit cards in Southeast Asia, Hangzhou-based DeepSeek chose a different path. In July 2024, Liang Wenfeng said in an interview with *Dark Surge*, "The problem we faced was never money, but the embargo on high-end chips." Later that year, DeepSeek released V3, completing training on 2048 H800 images, with the final training cost translating to approximately $5.576 million. The technical report stated that the entire training process "did not encounter any irrecoverable loss spikes, nor did it involve any rollbacks." On January 20, 2025, DeepSeek R1 was released, shaking the world with its inference capabilities brought by reinforcement learning. However, after R1, while its competitors went overseas to rent memory chips, DeepSeek did not move its main training operations abroad. A Financial Times report in November 2025 revealed that DeepSeek insisted on training domestically, with Huawei engineers stationed at its Hangzhou headquarters. The cost of staying put was real growing pains and waiting. In 2025, Huawei sent a team of engineers to DeepSeek's offices to assist it in training its next-generation inference model R2 on domestically produced Ascend chips. According to the Financial Times, training encountered problems such as stability issues and slow communication between software and chips, leading to repeated delays in the release of R2 and a corresponding postponement of the training schedule for the multimodal generative model. At the time, the outside world only saw DeepSeek slowing down, but few understood the groundwork it was laying underwater. In August 2025, DeepSeek released a transitional version, V3.1, stating in its release notes that the model used the UE8M0 FP8 precision format, specifically designed for "the upcoming next-generation domestically produced chip." On April 24, 2026, the long-awaited DeepSeek V4 was finally launched. The company stated in its announcement that due to limitations in high-end computing power, the service throughput of V4-Pro is limited, and the price will be reduced after the Ascend 950 supernode is mass-produced and launched in the second half of the year. Looking back in the fall of 2026, one company was scouring the globe for GPUs and integrating its models into the toolchains of global developers, while the other remained in China, relentlessly working on the underlying architecture and paving the way for domestically developed large-scale clusters. These two paths together formed the two wings of China's AI during its transition period. Until Washington decided to completely shut down the overseas market. At 4:15 PM, doors began closing one after another in the first two weeks of November 2026. First, it was just talk. On November 3rd, the Financial Times revealed that Nvidia's sales team began verbally informing global cloud service partners that at least 51% of capacity in newly signed contracts must be sold to non-Chinese customers. This requirement wasn't put on paper, but it left Southeast Asian data center owners bewildered. Where could they find so many non-Chinese customers outside the US? The following day, November 4th, Oracle cancelled a major five-year, approximately $7 billion deal with Tencent in Southeast Asia, involving about 100,000 chips. The deal fell through due to opposition from US officials. On November 12th, Jensen Huang, who had led Nvidia for 33 years, resigned as CEO amidst controversy. This Chinese entrepreneur, who had publicly stated that China's AI was "only a few nanoseconds behind the US" and bluntly said that US export controls were "largely counterproductive," left the game in this sensitive late autumn. On Monday, November 16th, at 4:15 PM Eastern Time, the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security submitted a provisional final rule to the Federal Register, titled "Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors." It was officially published on November 19th and took effect that same day.

New Regulations for Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors | Image Source: Government Website

Coincidentally, on the same day, US President Trump was attending the APEC Leaders' Informal Meeting in Shenzhen, and afterwards praised his "outstanding personal relationship" with Chinese leaders.

The core clause of the new regulations is only one: any data center in the world that provides more than 12 million TPPs of computing power to a company headquartered in China (including its overseas subsidiaries) must obtain a license from the US Department of Commerce in advance to transport advanced chips to that data center. 12 million TPPs, when converted, is roughly equivalent to 750 H100 chips, or about four or five server racks. Training a cutting-edge model with trillions of parameters requires thousands or even tens of thousands of cards. Four or five server racks wouldn't even be enough. For existing overseas data centers already serving Chinese customers, the new regulations provide a 90-day grace period to apply for licenses; otherwise, they "will face future export restrictions." Starting from November 19th, the 90-day deadline falls around February 17th, 2027. The new regulations include a presumption clause: if an overseas data center refuses to provide, or is unable to provide, customer due diligence information, this act itself will be considered a "red flag," and the exporter can be "presumed" to be "aware." In other words, if you can't say whose code is running in the data center, it's assumed you're problematic. Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil are specifically named; shipments of advanced AI chips to these five countries require permits and approvals. If the buyer is a company headquartered in the United States, the exporter can be exempted by submitting monthly reports. Physical supply disruptions follow closely behind. On November 17, during Nvidia's earnings call, Colette Kress, who succeeded Jensen Huang as interim CEO, confirmed: "We have stopped shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China." According to the Financial Times, TSMC and Samsung have also suspended shipments to some Chinese customers, pending licensing. The Chinese Ministry of Commerce expressed strong dissatisfaction and announced countermeasures; Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun stated bluntly that this was "a typical case of economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction." In the same week that the trade rules were implemented, financial leverage also began to tighten on Southeast Asian data centers. Many people believe that the proliferation of Neocloud in Southeast Asia is backed by wealthy conglomerates, but in reality, it's a capital-intensive business heavily reliant on debt. According to Bloomberg, since 2023, data center companies in the Asia-Pacific region have received approximately $49 billion in loans. A semiconductor industry research report estimates that 70-80% of Neocloud project funding comes from debt. A common practice is for data center owners to use long-term leases signed by major clients to borrow money from banks to buy Nvidia cards, then use the collected rental income to repay the principal and interest. In this chain, the deposit ratio is a barometer of geopolitical risk. In the overseas computing power market, the industry standard deposit for a typical customer renting an NVIDIA B300 server cluster is around 15%. However, when Dark Side of the Moon signed its $150 million B300 lease in Indonesia, it agreed to pay a 50% deposit upfront to secure the cards, which wouldn't be delivered until 2027. By early November, according to CNBC, when Dark Side of the Moon was negotiating to rent over 8,000 Blackwell chips in Europe, some even suggested it would have to pay 30% to 50% more in advance than non-Chinese customers. The new regulations implemented on November 19th directly deprived this premium of a counterparty. According to The Information, after the new regulations were introduced, Dark Side of the Moon cancelled the $150 million contract in Indonesia and suspended negotiations for other new deals. The overseas chips prepared for K4 were thus abandoned. Even more troublesome than the lease cancellation was the withdrawal of loans by banks. On November 17th, Bloomberg reported that a $480 million loan to Singaporean cloud service provider Aolani Cloud had been frozen. The money was originally intended to purchase Nvidia GPUs for a data center in Malaysia serving ByteDance. Previous reports indicated that the two companies had approximately 36,000 B200 loans in Malaysia. The lead bank for this loan was DBS Bank of Singapore. Following the announcement of the new regulations, five lenders began discussing withdrawing. Meanwhile, another cloud service provider, GMI Cloud, had previously borrowed $300 million in Thailand to build computing facilities to serve Tencent. The loan term sheet clearly stated that if Tencent were added to the US restricted list, the lenders had the right to demand early repayment. Southeast Asian governments are withdrawing under pressure to comply with regulations. Malaysian Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Johari Abdul Ghani told CNBC, "If you want to stay at the table, you have to follow the rules of the United States." Thailand's Deputy Minister of Commerce publicly stated that new projects not approved by the US "may not be completed." Singapore's Ministry of Digital Development and Information and Ministry of Trade and Industry issued a joint statement, "Companies will not be allowed to use their connections with Singapore to circumvent or violate the laws of other countries." The capital markets reacted quickly. On November 17th, two data center concept stocks on the Malaysian stock market plummeted nearly 20% intraday, and utility giant YTL Power fell nearly 10%. Meanwhile, on the same day in the Hong Kong market, SMIC surged 7%. In fact, long before Washington closed its doors, Beijing had already begun to proactively guide industries back to China. In September 2025, the Cyberspace Administration of China required companies like ByteDance and Alibaba to stop purchasing and testing NVIDIA's RTX Pro 6000D processors specifically designed for the Chinese market; in November, state-owned data center projects were required to use only domestically produced chips; and western provinces like Gansu, Guizhou, and Inner Mongolia, which are key hubs for computing power, provided data centers using domestically produced chips with electricity subsidies of up to half. Then, in January 2026, after the US conditionally allowed H200 flights, domestic customs informed customs brokers that H200 flights were "not permitted." On one hand, Washington is locking down overseas data centers; on the other hand, China is firmly closing the backdoor to specially supplied chips. Three years of external training and internal promotion have come to an end due to the two-way separation across the Pacific. Turning our attention back to China, to understand the urgency of this massive migration at the end of 2026, we must first see the other bittersweet ordeal that domestic laboratories are experiencing. User growth is too rapid, consuming all the cards used for research and development. At 0:11 AM on March 4, 2026, Lin Junyang, the technical lead for Alibaba's Qwen, posted a short line of English on X: "me stepping down. Bye my beloved qwen." Lin Junyang's departure was officially attributed to disagreements over the adjustment of responsibilities, with computing power merely a background factor. However, his complaints during an industry dialogue two months prior revealed the shared anxieties of many frontline technical leaders. He stated that simply handling daily deliveries consumed the majority of the team's computing power, leaving very little for cutting-edge research. ByteDance is also experiencing a similar internal struggle. By August 2026, according to LatePost, ByteDance had seriously discussed training a super model with over 5 trillion parameters. After reviewing its resources, it was found that its existing computing power reserves were "unable to support multi-threaded parallel research and development." The Seed team subsequently initiated internal architecture convergence. Why would even giants like ByteDance and Alibaba, who are not short of funds, feel that their computing power is insufficient? Because 2026 is the year when AI applications truly enter the daily lives of Chinese people. After the Spring Festival, the daily active users of ByteDance's Doubao app surpassed 200 million. High daily active users (DAU) bring high inference costs and operational pressure. Even ByteDance, traditionally adept at user acquisition and traffic optimization, reportedly has a very low budget for its Doubao app this year, according to 36Kr. Continuing to acquire new users will further strain its inference resources. In the large-scale model industry, pre-training and daily inference compete for the same pool of computing power. The more actively users engage with the model, the fewer computing resources are available for training the next generation. This "happy dilemma" is even more pronounced for startups. On February 16, 2026, after the release of Zhipu AI's flagship model GLM-5, the influx of concurrent requests exceeded the planned upper limit. Despite several previous expansions of its domestic chip cluster and restrictions on the sale of its Coding Plan packages, Zhipu's online services still experienced queues and lag. Zhipu was forced to publicly solicit chip manufacturers, computing power partners, and inference service providers. MiniMax, which does not build its own data centers and relies on cloud vendors for procurement, is also drastically increasing its budget. On August 26, 2026, MiniMax signed a supplementary agreement with Alibaba Cloud, raising its annual procurement caps for the three years from 2026 to 2028 from the original $115 million, $125 million, and $135 million to $300 million, $400 million, and $500 million, respectively. In an overseas podcast, founder Yan Junjie frankly admitted, "For us, especially for a Chinese AI company, computing power has always been a constraint." By September, even DeepSeek, known for its engineering efficiency, began redirecting user requests. It transferred requests that originally called V4-Pro to the newly released V4.1-Flash. On November 16th, "DeepSeek usage limit reached" trended on Weibo, with many heavy users hitting the limit in less than two hours of continuous use. Understanding this supply and demand relationship helps explain why there's a subtle sense of pent-up energy in the air in China during the second half of 2026. Over the past few months, various companies have been intensively iterating on minor versions and Flash models, but flagship models with ultra-high parameters have slowed down. Zhipu officially announced GLM-6 on August 31st, without giving a specific release date; MiniMax's Pro version with approximately 3 trillion parameters, reportedly planned for a Q3 release, has yet to appear; DeepSeek released V4.1-Flash, but not yet V4.1-Pro. Meanwhile, the API price war of two years ago, which disregarded costs, has completely subsided. Statistics show that in Q2 2026, the average input price of large model APIs in China was about 48% higher than in Q1 2025, and the output price was about 80% higher; DeepSeek's peak output price rose to 4.5 times its original level. Zhu Xiaohu once asserted, "This year may be the last year for foundational large-scale models." However, in our view, this conclusion reverses cause and effect. The slowdown in flagship model releases and the return of API prices to rationality are not because foundational models have reached their limits, but because China's large-scale models have moved out of the laboratory and truly entered hundreds of millions of real-world scenarios and the toolchains of global developers. According to statistics from research institution Epoch AI, from 2022 to mid-2026, China accounted for only about one-tenth of the global increase in AI computing power. However, statistics from Hugging Face, the world's largest open-source community, show that between February 2025 and February 2026, more than 40% of model downloads across all platforms came from models developed by Chinese teams. With only one-tenth of the global incremental computing power, China supported more than 40% of the global open-source model downloads and the daily use by hundreds of millions of people in China. Moreover, the rigid constraints of computing power have forced Chinese engineers to demonstrate their solid skills in architecture optimization and systems engineering. A Caixin-quoted industry expert judged that a small model, after deep tuning with harness, can achieve nearly 90% of the capabilities of a large model at about 4% of the cost. As Dylan Patel of SemiAnalysis commented a few days before the new regulations took effect in November: "In terms of capability, Dark Side of the Moon is probably as good as American labs; they just have significant gaps in computing power and deployment." Now, these engineers, who best understand how to conserve GPU resources, are collectively moving back to the foundation of domestically produced chips. Moving computing power from NVIDIA's CUDA ecosystem back to a domestically developed platform isn't a simple matter of issuing an administrative order; it's first and foremost an extremely demanding and meticulous undertaking of fundamental engineering challenges down to every single bit. In the words of chip and framework engineers, the first hurdle after returning home is "precision alignment." Ideally, with the same model architecture and the same batch of training data, running it on an NVIDIA GPU and running it on a Huawei Ascend NPU would produce two loss descent curves that fit perfectly together, like two sheets of tracing paper. However, in the real engineering world, even the slightest difference in the numerical precision of the underlying hardware or the reduction order of the communication operators can result in significant discrepancies between the two curves. iFlytek was one of the first Chinese companies to master this painstaking process. In its investor relations activity record from April 2026, iFlytek laid out the objective gap between the two generations of hardware. At that time, the Ascend 910B, which was its main product, had 64GB of single-card video memory, while the NVIDIA H200 had 141GB; the video memory bandwidth was 1.6TB/s on one side and 4.8TB/s on the other. In its unpacked state, iFlytek's training efficiency on the 910B cluster was only about 30% of that of a similarly sized NVIDIA A800 cluster. iFlytek collaborated deeply with Huawei, rewriting and optimizing each operator one by one. In 2025, they managed to increase the training efficiency of long-chain reinforcement learning from 30% to 84%, and the full-chain training efficiency of the Ascend native MoE model reached 93%. Even so, an objective adaptation period still existed. iFlytek recorded that when a new mainstream algorithm emerged internationally, it could be implemented directly on NVIDIA cards, but on domestically produced cards, it required additional solutions to a series of problems, such as optimizing the efficiency of the operator library, typically adding 3 to 6 months to the adaptation period. In October 2026, Liu Qingfeng, Chairman of iFlytek, said, "We don't want iFlytek to be the only one doing training on domestically produced computing power." Liu Qingfeng didn't have to wait too long. DeepSeek, which chose to stay put back then, has paved a significant step forward this autumn. Looking back, DeepSeek's R2 migration setback in 2025 was not a defeat, but rather a valuable trial run for the entire Chinese large-scale model industry. On the day DeepSeek V4 was released in April 2026, the Ascend chip immediately implemented inference support, and its expert parallel core kernel was validated on both NVIDIA and Ascend hardware. In July, a research team led by Huawei and including Shenzhen Hetao Academy disclosed that they had successfully completed full-parameter training of a DeepSeek V4-Pro 1.6 trillion-parameter model on a cluster of approximately 1,000 Ascend 910C GPUs. The training ran continuously for about a month, iterating over 1,500 times, with no skipped steps and no NaN errors. The model's computational utilization remained stable at 34.9%, with each step taking 27 seconds. On September 30th, the day before National Day, DeepSeek officially announced the open-sourcing of a complete set of underlying core components for the Ascend platform, from the TileLang compilation tool and computing libraries to the distributed communication library, all corresponding to the NVIDIA versions. To accommodate the memory access characteristics of domestically produced chips, DeepSeek even proactively modified the KV cache memory layout in its signature FlashMLA attention implementation, packaging the values ​​and scaling factors together, just to reduce the number of memory transfers for the Ascend chip. In the past Silicon Valley paradigm, modeling companies always wrote code according to the hardware architecture defined by NVIDIA; but in Hangzhou in 2026, a top modeling lab began to proactively reconstruct its underlying operators to suit the characteristics of domestically produced chips. Furthermore, Huawei and DeepSeek are jointly building a 128-card supernode based on the Ascend 950. SemiAnalysis' labs lit up and tested a Huawei Ascend 950PR test chip this year. It consumed 203.3 watts, had a core temperature of 56 degrees Celsius, and used just over 5GB of the 128GB HBM high-bandwidth memory. Under full load, it consumed approximately 600 watts. In computationally intensive matrix multiplication, which is the most demanding task, its measured utilization reached 41.5% of the theoretical limit. For comparison, NVIDIA's classic H100 achieves 46.8%. Besides DeepSeek, the entire Chinese large-scale model fleet is undergoing a complete overhaul of its underlying code. Kimi K3, from the dark side of the moon, introduced quantization-aware training from the supervised fine-tuning stage; Zhipu's GLM-5 completed adaptation to seven domestic chips, including Huawei Ascend, Cambricon, Hygon, and Kunlun Chip, on its first day of release; in the code repositories of various laboratories, pure CUDA operators are becoming increasingly rare, while cross-platform implementations like TileLang are becoming more common. These two technological trees on opposite sides of the Pacific are growing their own independent root systems from the most basic precision formats and memory layouts. Winter in Ulanqab On February 17, 2022, four departments, including the National Development and Reform Commission, jointly issued a document to launch the construction of national computing power hub nodes in eight regions: Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei, the Yangtze River Delta, the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area, Chengdu-Chongqing, Inner Mongolia, Guizhou, Gansu, and Ningxia. Ten national data center clusters were also planned, marking the full launch of the "East Data, West Computing" project. History sometimes presents astonishing coincidences. Almost exactly five years later, on the same day, around February 17, 2027, coincides with the 90-day deadline set by new US regulations for existing overseas data centers. Five years ago, when the document listed place names from the west and north such as Helingeer, Qingyang, Gui'an, and Zhongwei, many people thought it was just a routine energy allocation project. Land and energy resources in the east were becoming increasingly scarce, while the west and the north had endless winds and scorching sun. Furthermore, I always believe that we don't need to pay too much attention to the short-term movements of external funds. Most funds (whether retail investors or institutions, internal or external) are profit-driven, and these funds have never been the key force or fundamental driving force for the development of a technological ecosystem.

So I basically don't pay attention to popular opinions, and I don't focus much on the movements of large funds anymore. Their inherent short-term profit-seeking nature means that once the crypto ecosystem becomes profitable, they enter faster than anyone else, and turn their backs faster than flipping a book. To see if the core driving force and driving force of an ecosystem are still there, I only look at whether, during the ecosystem's lowest and most difficult times, there are still teams and core members still working hard and persevering. As long as these forces are still there, innovation is accumulating, the foundation is being strengthened, and one day, new flowers and fruits will surely reappear. As long as this remains unchanged, I have no worries at all. And in the current crypto ecosystem, I am very satisfied and reassured by the situation of these core members. 2. I remember your previous article saying that the A-shares market needed to reach 4000 points by the end of the year, otherwise it would be dangerous. data.title: Binance Wallet's Anthropic IPO, worth $500 million, only allocated 0.05% of its stake.
data.description:
Binance Wallet's Anthropic xStocks subscription reached 500 million USDC in less than 8 hours, with a final allocation ratio of approximately 0.05%.

Based on the offering price of $83, approximately 2,957 shares were worth only $245,000. Binance Wallet subsequently refunded the subscription funds in full, distributed these tokenized shares to participants for free, and also compensated users with $1 million worth of Anthropic tokenized shares ANTB.

One ​​user, X, suggested that Binance block xStocks and switch to another US stock IPO service provider.

Binance co-founder He Yi replied with four words: "Completely agree." On June 12th, SpaceX went public on Nasdaq. Binance, Bybit, and Bitget wallets all cancelled their respective tokenized IPOs on the same day because xStocks failed to secure enough shares from the offering process. It was reported that Binance refunded $557 million in subscription funds to 27,689 addresses. Five months later, it was Anthropic's turn. Binance Wallet opened for subscription on November 18th, with a total quota of 500 million USDC, plus a 5% xStocks service fee. The quota was filled nearly four hours ahead of schedule, and xStocks later stated that the overall oversubscription was more than 9 times. Ultimately, Binance Wallet was allocated only about 2,957 shares, worth about $245,000 based on the offering price of $83, accounting for 0.05% of the subscription amount. Binance's compensation plan involves a full refund of the subscription amount, a free airdrop of allocated shares to participants, and an additional $1 million worth of ANTB distributed to all applicants, guaranteeing a minimum of approximately $6 per person. This guaranteed minimum is slightly higher than the allocated value for 10,000 USDC subscribers. Gate announced that its Anthropic subscription totaled approximately 152 million USDT, with a final allocation of 92,100 shares, valued at approximately 7.644 million USDT, representing an allocation rate of approximately 5.03%. Bitget received a total of 153,774 shares. Of these, 137,494 shares were allocated in the VIP round (allocation rate of 10.06%), and 16,280 shares were allocated in the public round (allocation rate of 1.3%). Gate and Bitget did not use the same channels as Binance. Kraken, which also accessed xStocks IPO Access, did not disclose a uniform allocation rate; however, user reviews show that 1001 USDT received approximately 0.26 shares, equivalent to about 2.2%; for larger subscriptions of 500,000 to 1,000,000 USDT, the review rate was approximately 4%. The same xStocks platform did not ensure that all partner platforms received the same 0.05% allocation as Binance. The differences may stem from the platform's allocated quota, the size of the subscription pool, and xStocks' allocation method to different partners. Currently available public information is insufficient to determine which factor played a decisive role. However, Binance's problem is quite specific: it raised the activity cap to 500 million USDC, but only received $245,000 worth of shares. Regardless of how tight the overall upstream allocation is, this activity scale is severely imbalanced with the final supply capacity. After being blacklisted, what's next? xStocks is issued by Backed, a subsidiary of Payward, the parent company of Kraken, which is Binance's direct competitor. Binance Wallet is issuing ANTx under xStocks, and Kraken itself has also opened an ANTx subscription page. During the SpaceX event, several exchanges shared the same upstream pool: xStocks. However, Binance has no shortage of channels for tokenized stocks. On June 11th, Binance launched its own bStocks, issued by its affiliated company BTech Holdings, with the underlying shares purchased through Binance's licensed brokerage entity, Nest Trading Limited. Binance claims that by mid-October, bStocks' assets under management exceeded $1 billion, with a cumulative conversion of $6 billion. In its November 20th announcement, ANTB had already scheduled the launch of its spot trading platform. The missing piece is the next level: who will secure shares from the underwriting syndicate? Anthropic's underwriting syndicate is led by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, with 20 other investment banks participating. For retail investors, the US prospectus names six platforms: Charles Schwab, Fidelity, Robinhood, SoFi, Morgan Stanley's E*TRADE, and Trade-PMR. Anthropic has also published its brokerage firm lists in Australia, Canada, Japan, Switzerland, the UK, and parts of Europe. So, blacklisting xStocks at most eliminates one intermediary, allowing users to switch to bStocks or negotiate allocations directly with a brokerage or underwriter. Reportedly, Gate and BitMart did this with SpaceX, achieving a success rate of approximately 40%. Anthropic opened at $83 and rose to $111.50 on its first day, with users vying for the opportunity to be allocated shares at the offering price. Binance has proven its ability to gather 500 million USDC in hours; now it needs to prove whether its service providers can secure enough shares to meet this demand. Without improved distribution channels, even large subscription numbers will only amplify the embarrassment of the allocation results.

data.title: Lighter suffers $10.39 million theft: Signature nonce reuse vulnerability
data.description:
On November 16th, the decentralized perpetual contract trading platform Lighter experienced an abnormal outflow of approximately 10.39 million USDC. On November 17th, Lighter released an investigation report confirming that this large outflow was caused by the leakage of an API key from a trader's account. The key leakage was due to the trader using insecure signing code from an unofficial Lighter SDK. This code reused the signature nonce, allowing the private key to be recovered from public data. Beosin's analysis of this attack and the flow of stolen funds is as follows: I. Vulnerability and Attack Process Analysis Every transaction on Lighter is authorized by an API key signature. Each signature uses a one-time random value called a nonce, which must be unique and unpredictable each time. If two different transactions are signed using the same nonce and the same key, anyone can calculate the API key from the two signatures. Taking Schnorr signatures as an example, when the same key d is used to sign different messages s using nonce k, the result is as follows: s₁ = k + e₁d (mod q) s₂ = k + e₂d (mod q) Subtracting the two equations, the nonce is eliminated: s₁ − s₂ = (e₁ − e₂)d (mod q) Therefore, where e is the computable challenge value: = (s₁ − s₂)(e₁ − e₂)⁻¹ (mod q)

Attack flow:

(1) Because the API key can send funds to its own sub-accounts, and the public fund pool created by the account is also considered a sub-account. After the API key was leaked, the attackers first used the victim's key to create a public liquidity pool (2). Then, the attackers minted a large number of shares of this pool in accounts under their control (3). Funds from the affected accounts were transferred to the liquidity pool, increasing the net asset value without issuing new pool shares. From the platform's perspective, this was a normal internal transfer within the same address. It did not increase the number of shares or change the holder structure; the only result was an increase in the total assets of the pool. The number of shares remained the same, but the net value per share increased, allowing the attackers to profit. II. Tracing Stolen Funds According to Beosin Trace's analysis, after the attackers withdrew approximately 10.39 million USDC from the Lighter platform, they used the CoW Protocol to exchange all the USDC for approximately 5,400 ETH. Subsequently, they mainly transferred the funds to multiple addresses in amounts of 160 ETH per transaction: Of the confirmed stolen fund flows, approximately 800 ETH were exchanged for BNB through Thorchain, and approximately 299 ETH were exchanged for BTC through Thorchain. In addition, a total of 1920 ETH were exchanged for USDC on the Arbitrum network via the cross-chain bridge Li.Fi, and then deposited into Hyperliquid to purchase XMR spot. Currently, all attacker-related addresses have been flagged, and Beosin Trace will continue to monitor the movement of all stolen funds.

data.title: An epic pullback: What exactly happened?
data.description:
Author | Lone Ranger

Data Support | Gogudata (www.gogudata.com)

From 2022 to now, in four years, gold and silver have experienced an extreme cycle of epic soaring prices followed by an epic collapse.

The intensity of the fluctuations exceeded everyone's expectations.

In the futures market:

Gold rose 2.4 times from 370 yuan/gram at the beginning of 2022 to 1258 yuan/gram at the end of January this year, before falling to around 760 yuan/gram now, a drop of over 40%;

Silver rose 5.6 times from 48 yuan/gram at the beginning of 2022 to 320 yuan/gram at the end of January this year, before falling to around 100 yuan/gram now, a drop of over 70%;

The spot market prices have followed a similar pattern.

If you've been holding gold or silver for the past four years, even though you missed the peak, you'd still have at least doubled your investment, which is quite good. But in reality, how many people are like that? The vast majority exited early during the upward trend, missing out on the full gains. Even worse are those who entered too early during the downtrend, especially those with leverage. Leveraging their long positions in gold and silver almost inevitably leads to margin calls and forced liquidation. News about this has been circulating in the industry for months. This market cycle has truly taught everyone a lesson: the capital market never follows a fixed script; human calculations ultimately cannot withstand cyclical shifts. The bull market in precious metals that reached its peak in 2022 was driven by three narratives: Central bank gold purchases and reserve diversification were slow-moving variables that supported the bottom, but did not drive the main upward trend; the real driver of elasticity was the expectation of Fed rate cuts pushing down real interest rates; silver outperformed gold by benefiting from the industrial growth brought about by the expansion of photovoltaics and AI computing power, which was the core reason why silver significantly outperformed gold in the previous two years. However, central bank gold purchases can only support the bottom, not stop the trend driven by interest rates. The sharp drop in gold prices during the Fed's aggressive rate hikes in 2022 is a prime example. Even with continued increases in global central bank holdings, rising real interest rates still led to a valuation correction in gold. The seeds of the turning point were sown in the Middle East conflict in February of this year. Traditionally, geopolitical conflict equates to buying gold as a safe haven. However, this time the transmission chain has completely changed: the conflict first pushed up oil prices, oil prices increased inflation stickiness, and inflation stickiness forced the Federal Reserve to postpone interest rate cuts or even reprice interest rate hikes. Subsequently, geopolitics was no longer a boon for gold, but rather became a transmission channel for negative impacts on precious metals—what the market calls a safe-haven backlash. The reversal of expectations happened gradually. In the first half of the year, the market was still speculating that interest rate cuts would only be postponed. The real watershed moment came in the third quarter, when pricing completely shifted from waiting for interest rate cuts to maintaining high interest rates for longer, coupled with another round of risks. The direct trigger for the market was the higher-than-expected CPI in September, at 3.7% year-on-year and 0.6% month-on-month. Gasoline and commodity prices pushed inflation back up, oil prices rose for four consecutive months, and inflation stickiness led more and more Federal Reserve officials to quickly turn hawkish. On November 18th, Waller, who had previously leaned dovish, publicly shifted to a hawkish stance, stating that a single 50bp rate hike in December was worth considering if inflation continued to worsen. The subsequent October meeting minutes were even more hawkish, with the vast majority of officials acknowledging further room for tightening, and some considering a December rate hike exceeding 25bp reasonable. Consequently, funding costs worsened, with the probability of a 25bp hike in December exceeding 95%, and the tail risk of a 50bp hike being factored in. Traders began betting on another 50bp hike in January. The US dollar index also surged again to 103, a 19-month high, with the 10-year Treasury yield holding above 5.1% and the 2-year yield at 4.80%. Faced with a combination of higher-than-5% risk-free returns over a longer period, coupled with a stronger dollar suppressing pricing, and non-interest-bearing precious metals, funds had no choice but to exit the market.

02 The other straw that broke the camel's back was the AI ​​narrative crisis.

Since July, from the controversy surrounding the circular financing of tech giants, to the bursting of the bubble in South Korea's Samsung and SK Hynix, and then to the Huang Renxun incident and Intel's earnings disappointment, the ongoing controversy surrounding AI capital expenditure has accelerated the pullback in global stock markets.

This led to a correction in tech stocks, breaking through the margin requirements of leveraged funds. Investors needed to raise cash to cover their positions, and gold, with its best liquidity and fastest conversion to cash, became the asset to be sold first—selling gold to save tech stocks.

This selling was indiscriminate of price. After a rapid breakdown, a chain of technical stop-loss orders emerged, further amplifying the sharp drop.

Similar scenes have been common in the past few years.

Silver suffered an additional blow.

Since the beginning of this year, the market has lowered its forecasts for global AI capital expenditure and data center construction, coupled with the continued implementation of photovoltaic silver reduction technology, causing the two major industrial narratives supporting silver to be revised downwards simultaneously.

More than half of silver demand comes from industry, with photovoltaics being the largest contributor to this growth over the past five years. The use of silver in silver paste, copper-coated silver, and silver-free pastes continues to reduce silver consumption per watt. Institutional estimates predict that silver demand for photovoltaics will decline by 21%–30% in 2026, leading to a roughly 5% reduction in total annual silver demand. Market focus has shifted from long-term shortages to oversupply. Furthermore, the small size of the silver market and the crowded speculative long positions created by earlier buying have resulted in concentrated stop-loss orders, leading to a negative feedback loop of price declines, triggered stop-loss orders, and further declines. Fund flows also confirm this pattern. Global gold ETFs saw continuous reductions of hundreds of tons in holdings during the first half of the year, while silver ETF holdings decreased by 4% by early November compared to the beginning of the year. In addition, institutions have recently lowered their targets. Goldman Sachs lowered its gold price target for the second time this month, reducing its year-end 2027 target from $4,800 to $4,650. This downward revision of sell-side expectations continues to suppress bullish sentiment.

03 ​​So, when will gold and silver see a turnaround?

The most fundamental anchor remains the US dollar interest rate.

And the turning point of interest rates depends first on inflation. Whether CPI, core CPI, and PPI can fall back, and whether oil and energy prices can stop rising, are prerequisites for the Fed to turn dovish.

The two most direct indicators are the 10-year US Treasury real yield and the US dollar index. As long as real interest rates continue to rise, the cost pressure of holding gold will not decrease.

In addition to macro interest rates, we also need to look at liquidity clearing.

Only when the leveraged liquidation of tech stocks ends and the pressure of passive selling across assets is completely released will gold stop being used as a cash ATM.

For silver, we also need to look at signals such as the clearing of speculative long positions, the return of ETF funds, the stabilization of expected silver demand for photovoltaics, and the upward revision of expected AI capital expenditure.

The medium- to long-term bottom support has not disappeared. The demand for credit hedging brought about by central bank gold purchases and fiscal deficits is still there. It's just that this slow variable has lost its pricing power in the short term in a high real interest rate environment. Therefore, in the short term, although the decline in the past few days has been terrifying, it is not advisable to rush to buy the dip. The real turning point will have to wait until the expectation of interest rate hikes peaks, real interest rates fall, short positions are cleared, and expectations stabilize. 04 Epilogue This round of gold and silver market frenzy and collapse has taught us not only whether the logic of precious metals has broken down, but also a set of disciplines for survival. Using the logic of slow variables to leverage fast variables is the most expensive mismatch in this market. As Keynes said, the market can remain irrational for longer than you can remain solvency. Therefore, never use leverage to prove a judgment that may be delayed but is correct. Because even the strongest long-term logic often cannot withstand short-term margin calls. Investing is not about proving yourself right, but about maintaining solvency in a highly uncertain market until the logic proves correct.

data.title: Before the Wall Street bell-ringing ceremony | On-chain answer already given: The truth about the Anthropic price spread
data.description: At 11:48 AM Eastern Time on November 19, 2026, the Nasdaq opening bell rang for Anthropic (stock code: ANT). After a two-hour and eighteen-minute pre-market auction, the first traded price settled at $111.50, a 34.3% increase from the offering price of $83, briefly pushing its market capitalization past the $2 trillion mark. With its initial fundraising of $81.34 billion, Anthropic surpassed SpaceX, setting a new record for the highest-grossing IPO in global capital markets. Just one minute before the official opening, the pre-market price for ANT contracts on the decentralized perpetual contract trading platform Hyperliquid stopped at $111. Two seemingly unrelated markets differed in price by a mere 50 cents. Overnight, the crypto market appeared to have taken over Wall Street's pricing power. But behind this tiny 50-cent difference lies a truth far more complex than "precise pricing." Before Wall Street even opened, the blockchain was already a frenzy. In the past, unicorn IPOs were a highly closed game. Investment banks handled the book-building, institutional investors received the majority of the allocation, and ordinary investors could only trade after the stock was listed. Company valuations could rise steadily in the primary market, but a publicly available, continuous, and participatory price often only appeared on the day of the listing. Pre-market contracts are rewriting this order. Glassnode data shows that Anthropic's cumulative pre-market contract notional trading volume in the 45 days leading up to its IPO reached a staggering $9.5 billion, a 144% increase compared to SpaceX's $3.9 billion during the same period, setting a new record for pre-market trading. According to Castle Labs data, as of November 19th, the 24-hour trading volume of the Anthropic pre-market contract on Entropy.io alone on Hyperliquid reached approximately $531 million, with open interest reaching $496 million at one point, nearly double the peak open interest before SpaceX's IPO. A new market division of labor is emerging. Wall Street still controls stock issuance and allocation, while the crypto market has taken over the role of "pre-market trading." Before the official opening of the stock market, it allows global investors to buy and sell unicorn price expectations using stablecoins. IPOs are no longer just a game of price inquiries and allocations among institutional investors, but are beginning to become an open and continuous trading market. The truth behind the 0.2% error: "Copying homework" from Nasdaq. While the pre-market market is rapidly expanding, the price difference between on-chain contracts and traditional markets seems to be narrowing significantly. According to calculations by Eliezer Ndinga, Head of Research at 21Shares, the pre-market price of ANT contracts on Hyperliquid differed from its Nasdaq first-minute trading price by only 0.2%, and the average price difference between the two further narrowed to about 0.1% after the opening. Even using the official Nasdaq opening price of $111.50, the error was only 0.5%. If you only observe the two minutes before and after the opening, the crypto market seems to have completed "precise pricing" before Nasdaq. But if you extend the timeline, the story changes. At 4:35 PM Eastern Time on November 18th, the night before the IPO pricing, the pre-market ANT contract on Hyperliquid was still around $98, 12.11% below the opening price the next day. It wasn't until the morning of November 19th that Nasdaq's auction window began releasing price signals at $100, $104, and $110, and the on-chain price followed suit, finally reaching $110.48 four minutes before the opening (11:44 AM Eastern Time), 0.91% below the first traded price. The price difference within 1% is less a sign of the crypto market having foresight and more a result of traders meticulously tracking the Nasdaq pre-market auction on Bloomberg terminals. It's more like a cross-market information relay rather than a one-sided pre-pricing by the crypto market. In the early stages of pre-market contracts, prices reflected a vague consensus in the market regarding the valuation of the underlying asset. As prospectuses, offering price ranges, and oversubscription results during roadshows were gradually disclosed, market expectations were continuously revised. During the call auction phase, the real-time price indication from the traditional market became the most direct anchor, guiding pre-market prices to converge. The so-called "precise pricing" in the crypto market essentially means that it opened a tradable market earlier, and subsequently, as information became more transparent, prices continued to converge towards the true price. Pre-market market performance: Correct direction doesn't guarantee accurate price. Anthropic's "perfect synchronization" is more like an exceptional case than a replicable pattern. Looking back at historical pre-IPO cases, pre-market contracts haven't performed as well as ANT. Of the eight IPOs analyzed by Grayscale, pre-market contracts achieved a 7/8 accuracy rate in predicting the opening direction on the first day. All five stocks that Trade.xyz completed conversions also conformed to the pattern of "issue price lower than the previous night's contract price, opening price higher than the issue price." From a directional perspective, pre-market contracts serve as a reliable "sentiment thermometer." However, when applied to price, the error becomes dramatically amplified. The most typical counterexample is SpaceX. On the eve of its IPO in June, the SpaceX pre-market contract on Hyperliquid closed at $172.84, implying a 28% first-day gain; however, the Nasdaq opened at only $150 the following day, meaning the contract still deviated from the actual opening price by about 6% even in the last minute before opening. Cerebras and Quantumuum performed even worse, remaining deeply trapped below their IPO prices for extended periods after listing. Even Anthropic, after opening high at $111.50, quickly fell back, closing its first day at $97.17. If an average investor had focused on the on-chain price of $110 and rushed into the Nasdaq opening price, they would have suffered a 12.85% unrealized loss in just four hours. The most memorable aspect of Anthropic's listing day wasn't the small price difference of less than 1% in the pre-market market. The crypto market hasn't proven itself to know better than Wall Street how much an AI giant is worth, but it has transformed the previously closed IPO pricing process, accessible only to a select few, into an open, continuous market where everyone can participate. The debate over the value of a unicorn is no longer confined to investment banks' closed-door roadshows. This is an extension of pricing power; Wall Street issues the shares, while the crypto market trades in the anticipation. Ultimately, the answer lies in the real money after the market opens. (Author: Jae, PANews)

data.title: South Korean Man Accused Of Using AI To Cheat In Law Entrance Exam Found Dead At Seoul Motel
data.description:
A South Korean man who gained public attention for achieving a perfect score in a national law school entrance examination has been found dead at a motel in Seoul, hours before he was due to livestream a test to defend himself against allegations of AI-assisted cheating.

Lee Jin-woo, 32, was found unconscious at a motel near Cheonho Station on 19 November after failing to appear for the scheduled livestream.

Lee Jin-woo, 32, had promised to solve the national college entrance exam live on November 19 to prove his abilities & address cheating allegations

— GlobeUpdate (@Globupdate) November 19, 2026

Perfect Exam Results Sparked AI Cheating Suspicions

Lee's academic achievements attracted attention after he went from performing poorly in South Korea's College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT) to scoring almost perfectly in 2025 and gaining admission to Seoul National University's dentistry programme.

He later achieved a perfect score in the 2026 Legal Education Eligibility Test (LEET), published a book titled "Brain Accelerator" and began coaching students preparing for examinations.

However, suspicions emerged after viewers noticed unusual answer corrections in his LEET examination booklet, which he showed on a YouTube channel in October.

The pattern raised speculation that he might have copied answers from an external source, potentially AI, although this did not establish that cheating had occurred.

Questions also emerged over his previous examination results, prompting further scrutiny of his academic claims.

Lee Failed To Appear For Public Livestream

Lee had agreed to solve Korean-language questions from the 2026 CSAT in real time to prove his abilities.

The livestream was scheduled for 8am on 19 November and attracted more than 400,000 viewers.

He had told a media outlet the previous evening,

"I will demonstrate my abilities through a public test and put the allegations to rest."

However, he failed to arrive, and organisers cancelled the exercise at 8:35am.

It did not mention the cheating allegations or contain an apology.

Police said an autopsy and further investigations would establish the cause of death.

The controversy also brought attention to Lee's previous criminal convictions.

He later received an additional six-month sentence for repeating similar offences against five people.

Before his death, two criminal complaints had been filed over allegations that he used AI to cheat in the CSAT and LEET, potentially falsified examination records and misled buyers of his study book and services.

Although Lee's death is expected to end criminal proceedings against him, South Korean police said they would continue investigating the allegations and whether anyone else was involved.

The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency said the investigation would continue "to confirm the substantive truth".

data.title: What does Democratic control of Congress mean for digital assets after the midterm elections?
data.description:
Author: Katrina Paglia, Chief Legal Officer of Pantera; Source: Pantera November Blockchain Investor Letter; Compiled by: Jinse Finance Claw

The Democrats won control of both houses of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections, flipping the House and taking the Senate by a large margin—multiple media outlets have called it one of the biggest seat swings in decades.

This result was primarily driven by economic issues and the aftermath of the Iran war, with digital asset policy being a secondary factor, but it has reshaped the political landscape of the entire industry; and the industry's core legislative priority—a federal market structure bill—has been under negotiation in this landscape for nearly three years.

Source: Digital asset position ratings from Stand With Crypto, as of November 16, 2026; unrated members are listed as "Unrated". Election results and house seats are from the Associated Press, as of 3:09 PM ET on November 19, 2026. Senate counts include two independent senators operating with the Democratic caucus. Stand With Crypto's party-to-party data may differ from the Associated Press count by one House seat. What Changes Have Occurred in Congress? As of November 19, the Associated Press reported that Democrats won 257 seats in the House of Representatives, Republicans 172, and 6 seats remain undecided. Hakeem Jeffries is expected to succeed Mike Johnson as Speaker. In the Senate, the Associated Press reported that Democrats held 56 seats (including two independent senators operating with the Democratic caucus) and Republicans 44. This result gives Democrats control of the House Financial Services Committee and the Senate Banking Committee for the last two years of the Trump administration—these two committees are responsible for drafting legislation on the structure of the digital asset market. However, Trump retains the power to veto any bill submitted to the president's desk. The new Congress is also unusually inexperienced. When the 120th Congress is sworn in on January 3, 2027, at least 120 of the 535 seats in the House and Senate (approximately 22%, which could rise as the results of the final few elections are announced) will be filled by newly elected members, representing one of the largest groups of newly elected members in decades. This personnel change has both advantages and disadvantages, but overall it is a mildly positive for the industry. A significant portion of the newly elected members have no voting history on digital asset issues and do not possess the deeply entrenched, personally hostile stances of some outgoing members; this allows for greater flexibility in developing sound policies from scratch, rather than engaging in battles with established opposition forces.

A New Path for the CLARITY Act

The Digital Asset Market Clarity Act passed the House of Representatives by a large margin in July 2025 with bipartisan support, but stalled in the Senate Banking Committee due to ethical provisions concerning the president's and members' personal digital asset holdings; Democratic senators such as Kirsten Gillibrand have warned about this for months.

Now that Democrats control both houses, the bill is unlikely to advance with the existing version already passed in the House. It has been reported that House Democrats are discussing expanding Representative Maxine Waters' Crypto Investors Consumer Rights Act into their own broader market structure framework, rather than abandoning the effort altogether.

The industry's investment of approximately $233 million in the midterm elections did not translate into lasting control over the outcome; the potential terms of any final agreement—including stronger conflict-of-interest provisions for the president and a greater emphasis on investor protection compared to the CFTC-centric approach of the House bill—are likely to shift in the Democratic direction. Other regulatory clues to watch: Not everything is in flux. The GENIUS Act—the stablecoin framework to be signed into law in 2025—is already in place, and its implementing rules at the Treasury and banking regulator levels will continue to be developed regardless of which party controls Congress. The Senate's power to confirm the leadership of the SEC and CFTC now rests with committees controlled by Democrats, which will impact the next round of committee vacancies, but will not change the current Trump-appointed agency heads before 2029. The more direct impact lies in the tone. A Congress focused on overseeing the current administration's own digital asset initiatives (including the president's meme and token projects) is likely to maintain this scrutiny through hearings and investigations, even if it fails to legislate—a point several Democrats have cited as a reason for the breakdown in market structure negotiations. What does this mean for crypto? The baseline scenario is delay and renegotiation, not a reversal. The stablecoin framework has been maintained, but comprehensive federal market structure legislation—the rulebook that will ultimately clarify the SEC and CFTC's jurisdiction over most tokens—seems unlikely to pass before the next Congress convenes in 2027, and is likely to be delayed even further. This means the current landscape, cobbled together by SEC enforcement, CFTC jurisdiction, and state-level money transfer laws, will persist longer than the industry expects. Therefore, we should continue to assess and place new positions according to existing rules (rather than the rules we expect to arrive soon). We will continue to monitor the House Democrats' market structure alternatives and the development of ethics provisions in the next Congress.

data.title: Solana validators decreased by 64% in less than three years: Decentralization is no longer a necessity.
data.description:
Author: r2Jamong Source: X, @r2Jamong Translation: Shan Ouba, Jinse Finance

Solana's active validator count has decreased by 64% in less than three years, from 1,963 on December 28, 2023 to 701 on November 15, 2026. However, the Solana Foundation continues to scale back the delegation program that once helped maintain the validator base. Are the long-standing goals of decentralization and wider distribution in blockchain networks losing their appeal?

Focus of Exits Contributed to Validators with Less Staking

Of the 1,963 validators who held staked data in December 2023, 1,713 left. Of the 701 validators supporting the network at the end of the period, 250 were from the original group, and 451 were newcomers. To determine what these exits mean for a Proof-of-Stake (PoS) network, it's necessary to understand two things simultaneously: how many validators left, and what happened to their staking.

Of the top 100 validators by staking volume in December 2023, only 12 left. None of these 12 voting accounts registered the operator's name, so some operators may have simply changed accounts. Of the 1,663 validators ranked 301st and below, 95% have left, with most small validators relying on small staking amounts shutting down their nodes.

During the same period, Solana's total staking volume increased by approximately 11%, from 387.2 million SOL to 429.33 million SOL. The proportion of staking to total supply remained almost unchanged, slightly decreasing from approximately 68% to 67%.

The Foundation reduced delegation of approximately 41 million SOL, meaning that staking from other sources increased by approximately 83 million SOL.

Measured by the number of validators, Solana became less decentralized and less decentralized; however, the security it gained from staking SOL remained.

Foundation Reduces Delegation Program

Including validators who joined and left during the period, a total of 2,576 validators left. Of these, 1,280 had staked less than 20% of their peak amount before ceasing operations. Loss of delegated staking directly reduces revenue and makes it harder to cover node operating costs. Given Solana's high hardware requirements, a decline in revenue is enough to force a validator to shut down.

Of the departing validators, 1,243 held between 50,000 and 100,000 SOL at their peak. Staking rankings provide clues as to why so many validators maintained this level. In December 2023, approximately 70% of the total staking by the 700 validators ranked 301st to 1000th came from the Solana Foundation Delegated Program (SFDP). The way the Foundation allocates staking may also explain why a large number of validators in this group held between 60,000 and 70,000 SOL. The timing of these exits also coincides with adjustments to the Foundation's delegation rules. The first half of 2024 saw 865 exits, the highest number for a half-year. The revised rules took effect on the 578th epoch in February 2024. In the second half of 2025, another 451 validators left. In October of that year, the foundation began reducing the matching ratio from 1:1 to 0.5:1, and the matching cap from 100,000 SOL to 50,000 SOL. According to the foundation, SFDP's share of total staking had decreased from approximately 44.4% at launch to approximately 5.9% in November 2025. This trend illustrates that as the foundation reduces staking subsidies, validators who cannot attract sufficient external staking or maintain operations through self-delegation are gradually leaving the system. Validators who are most unable to replace foundation-delegated operators with their own SOL or external delegation are also the most likely to fail to sustain their nodes. What does a mature PoS network look like? What exactly do distribution and decentralization mean? A network with more validators has a wider physical distribution and a higher degree of decentralization. However, if most of their staking comes from the same foundation, political power remains centralized. On Solana, the foundation's staking share has decreased significantly, while staking outside the foundation is increasing. In this sense, power distribution is broader than before. The network is less decentralized in terms of the number of nodes, but the power to decide "who can afford to be a validator" has shifted from the foundation to the market. With the decrease in the proportion of staking provided by the foundation, validators rely more on the SOL they can stake and the delegation they obtain from others. As PoS networks mature, external delegators will naturally take over the foundation's role in early supply staking.

The Old Narrative of Distribution and Decentralization

For many, decentralization and distribution have long been the standards for measuring the value of blockchains. Today, both as ends in themselves are losing weight.

Among the densely emerging layer-one blockchains, only a few have survived. Each survivor can give its own unique reasons, and they now see relying on these distinctive advantages as the best opportunity for survival.

Trustlessness and censorship resistance remain Ethereum's highest priorities, and Ethereum already has means beyond decentralization and distribution to maintain these two points.

It has already reduced the number of validators through validator consolidation; after transitioning to zero-knowledge (ZK) proofs, a small number of operators with high-performance hardware will handle most of the block production and proof generation. As long as trustlessness and censorship resistance remain, Ethereum has little reason to decentralize every part of the network. Solana aims to build an internet capital market where people can trade any asset. Such markets require infrastructure operators capable of maintaining low latency and high throughput even during surges in transaction volume. Maintaining a large validator set involves costs and trade-offs, and Solana has chosen to bear fewer costs than in the past. Distribution and decentralization once provided blockchain networks with a way to prove "why people need it." As the hype subsided, networks found other reasons to use them and began to recalculate the true value of decentralization. Decentralization is no longer a creed for every blockchain.
